title: Magnesium — calm nerves, steady energy, restful sleep
text: Magnesium is a cofactor in over 300 enzymatic reactions, including ATP energy production, muscle relaxation, and regulation of the nervous system — which is why it's commonly linked to steadier stress response and more restful sleep. It also supports healthy blood pressure and bone structure alongside calcium and vitamin D. Whole-food sources are rich and varied: leafy greens (spinach, chard), pumpkin seeds, almonds, cashews, black beans and other legumes, whole grains, avocado, and dark chocolate. Because magnesium sits at the center of chlorophyll, deeply green vegetables are a reliable marker of magnesium content. Absorption can be modestly reduced by very high-phytate diets (large amounts of unsoaked whole grains/legumes) or by high alcohol intake, and gut conditions that cause chronic diarrhea (like poorly managed IBS or Crohn's) can lower levels over time. People who commonly run low, educationally speaking, include those eating a lot of refined/processed food (which strips magnesium during processing), older adults (reduced absorption), people with type 2 diabetes (increased urinary losses), and those under chronic stress or heavy training load. Soaking, sprouting, or fermenting grains and legumes can modestly improve mineral availability. Food-first approaches — a handful of pumpkin seeds, a serving of black beans, a big spinach salad — are a gentle, sustainable way to support intake; talk to your provider before supplementing, especially alongside kidney disease or certain medications.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Vitamin D — the sunshine nutrient for bones, immunity, and mood
text: Vitamin D functions more like a hormone than a classic vitamin: it supports calcium absorption and bone mineralization, plays a role in modulating immune function, and is linked to mood regulation. Unlike most micronutrients, the body can synthesize it when skin is exposed to UVB sunlight, which is why 'the sunshine vitamin' is a common nickname — but food and supplementation matter for anyone with limited sun exposure. Whole-food sources are relatively few: fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring), egg yolks, and UV-exposed mushrooms provide meaningful amounts; fortified foods like milk, plant milks, and some orange juices add more in many diets. Because dietary sources are limited, vitamin D status is closely tied to geography, season, skin tone, sun exposure habits, and age — people who commonly watch their levels include those living at higher latitudes or with limited sun exposure, people with darker skin (which reduces UVB-driven synthesis), older adults (skin synthesizes less efficiently with age), people who are consistently sun-avoidant or covered, exclusively breastfed infants, and those with fat-malabsorption conditions since vitamin D is fat-soluble and best absorbed alongside dietary fat. Pairing vitamin D-containing foods with a source of healthy fat (olive oil, avocado, nuts) may support absorption. Blood testing is the only reliable way to know individual status — talk to your provider before supplementing, since it is fat-soluble and can accumulate.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Iron — heme vs. non-heme, and why vitamin C makes plant iron work harder
text: Iron supports oxygen transport (as a core component of hemoglobin) and cellular energy production, which is why sustained low intake is often associated with fatigue and reduced stamina. Dietary iron comes in two forms with very different absorption profiles: heme iron, found in animal foods (red meat, poultry, fish, oysters), is absorbed efficiently and consistently by the body; non-heme iron, found in plant foods (lentils, beans, tofu, spinach, pumpkin seeds, fortified cereals) and also in animal foods, is absorbed less efficiently and is more sensitive to what it's eaten with. This is where pairing matters: vitamin C-rich foods — citrus, bell peppers, strawberries, tomatoes, broccoli — eaten in the same meal can meaningfully enhance non-heme iron absorption by helping keep it in a more absorbable form. Conversely, coffee, tea (tannins), and calcium-rich foods eaten at the same meal can reduce non-heme iron uptake, so spacing them apart from iron-rich meals is a common practical tip. People who commonly run low, educationally, include menstruating women, pregnant people, endurance athletes, frequent blood donors, infants and toddlers during rapid growth, and those eating primarily plant-based diets without deliberate vitamin C pairing. A simple food-first pattern — lentils with a squeeze of lemon, spinach salad with bell pepper and citrus dressing — supports better uptake. Iron status is best assessed via bloodwork; talk to your provider before supplementing, as excess iron is not benign.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Vitamin B12 — nerve function, energy, and red blood cell formation
text: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) supports the formation of healthy red blood cells, DNA synthesis, and the maintenance of the nervous system's protective myelin sheath — functions that make it central to steady energy and healthy nerve signaling. Unlike most micronutrients, B12 is reliably found only in animal-derived foods: meat, poultry, fish, shellfish (especially clams), eggs, and dairy. Fortified foods — nutritional yeast, some plant milks, and fortified cereals — are the main route for those who don't eat animal products. Absorption is a multi-step process requiring stomach acid to release B12 from food protein and intrinsic factor (made in the stomach) to carry it into the bloodstream, which is why absorption efficiency, not just intake, matters. People who commonly watch their B12 status, educationally, include plant-based and vegan eaters (the most direct dietary gap), older adults (age-related decline in stomach acid, called atrophic gastritis, reduces absorption even with adequate intake), people on long-term acid-reducing medications, those with gut conditions affecting absorption (Crohn's, celiac, prior bariatric surgery), and pregnant or breastfeeding people on plant-based diets, since B12 is essential for the developing nervous system. Because B12 deficiency can develop slowly and silently — sometimes masked by folate intake — it's a nutrient worth being deliberate about through fortified foods or bloodwork rather than assuming diet alone covers it. Talk to your provider before supplementing, and about periodic testing if you're in a higher-awareness group.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Zinc — immune resilience, wound repair, and taste/smell
text: Zinc is a structural and catalytic cofactor in hundreds of enzymes and plays a well-documented supportive role in immune cell development and function, wound healing, protein synthesis, and maintaining a healthy sense of taste and smell. Whole-food sources include oysters (exceptionally concentrated), red meat, poultry, pumpkin seeds, cashews, chickpeas, lentils, and whole grains. As with iron, zinc from plant sources is less bioavailable than from animal sources because phytates — naturally occurring compounds in grains, legumes, and seeds — bind zinc and reduce absorption. Traditional food preparation methods that reduce phytate content, such as soaking, sprouting, and leavening (as in traditional sourdough bread), can meaningfully improve zinc availability from plant foods. People who commonly run low, educationally, include those following primarily plant-based diets without these preparation methods, people with high alcohol intake (which increases urinary zinc losses), those with malabsorptive gut conditions (Crohn's, chronic diarrhea, celiac), and older adults, who both absorb less efficiently and often eat less zinc-dense food overall. Because zinc and copper compete for absorption pathways, and excess zinc from high-dose supplements can suppress copper status over time, a food-first approach — a handful of pumpkin seeds, chickpeas in a meal, occasional oysters or lean meat — is a gentler way to support intake than routine high-dose supplementation. Talk to your provider before supplementing, particularly at doses above typical multivitamin levels.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Omega-3s — EPA, DHA, and ALA for brain, heart, and inflammation balance
text: Omega-3 fatty acids support cell membrane structure, are precursors to specialized pro-resolving mediators involved in balancing inflammation, and are strongly linked with cardiovascular and brain health, particularly the long-chain forms EPA and DHA. There are three main dietary omega-3s, and the distinction matters: EPA and DHA are the 'active,' long-chain forms found directly in fatty fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel, anchovies, herring) and algae; ALA is a shorter-chain plant form found in flaxseed, chia seeds, walnuts, and hemp seeds, which the body can convert to EPA and DHA — but only inefficiently, typically well under 10-15% conversion in most people. This conversion inefficiency is central to food-first guidance: someone relying solely on flax or chia for omega-3s is not getting an equivalent supply to someone eating fatty fish. Algae-based DHA/EPA is a direct, non-fish route to the long-chain forms. Balance with omega-6 intake also matters functionally, since the modern diet (high in vegetable oils) skews heavily omega-6 dominant, which can shift the inflammatory balance; reducing processed seed-oil-heavy foods while increasing omega-3 sources helps restore ratio. People who commonly run low, educationally, include those who eat little to no fatty fish, strict vegans/vegetarians without algae-based sources, and people on diets very high in processed omega-6 oils. Two to three servings of fatty fish weekly, or a daily algae-DHA source for plant-based eaters, is a common food-first target; talk to your provider before supplementing, especially if on blood thinners.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements; Harvard T.H. Chan The Nutrition Source

title: Folate — cell division, DNA synthesis, and the natural-food-form advantage
text: Folate (vitamin B9) is essential for DNA synthesis and repair and for cell division, which is why it's especially emphasized around periods of rapid growth, most notably early pregnancy for neural tube development. It also works alongside B12 in one-carbon metabolism, supporting healthy homocysteine balance. Naturally occurring folate — the word literally derives from 'foliage' — is abundant in dark leafy greens (spinach, romaine, arugula), legumes (lentils, chickpeas, black beans), asparagus, avocado, and citrus fruits. 'Folate' refers to the natural food form; 'folic acid' is the synthetic form used in fortified grains and most supplements, and the two are processed by the body somewhat differently, which is a distinction some integrative practitioners consider worth understanding, particularly for the subset of people with reduced ability to convert folic acid efficiently (commonly discussed as MTHFR gene variation). Folate is heat- and water-sensitive, so light steaming or eating leafy greens raw preserves more than prolonged boiling. People who commonly watch folate status, educationally, include those planning pregnancy or in early pregnancy, people with high alcohol intake (which impairs folate metabolism), those with malabsorptive gut conditions, and people eating few leafy greens or legumes overall. A food-first pattern — a big salad, a serving of lentils or beans most days, occasional citrus — supports steady intake. Talk to your provider before supplementing, and about individualized folate-form guidance if pregnancy or genetic variation is relevant.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Calcium — bone structure, muscle signaling, and food-first sourcing
text: Calcium is best known for building and maintaining bone and tooth structure, but it also plays a supportive role in muscle contraction, nerve signaling, and healthy blood clotting. Dairy (milk, yogurt, cheese) is a concentrated, well-absorbed source, but plant sources can meaningfully contribute too: fortified plant milks, tofu made with calcium sulfate, sesame seeds/tahini, almonds, white beans, and cooked leafy greens like bok choy, kale, and collards. A useful nuance: some leafy greens — spinach and chard in particular — are high in calcium on paper but also high in oxalates, which bind calcium and sharply limit its absorption, so they shouldn't be relied on as a primary calcium source the way lower-oxalate greens (kale, bok choy, collards) can be. Calcium works as part of a team — vitamin D supports its absorption, vitamin K supports directing it to bone rather than soft tissue, and magnesium supports the enzymes that activate vitamin D — so food-first strategies typically pair calcium-rich foods with these cofactors rather than viewing calcium in isolation. People who commonly watch calcium intake, educationally, include those avoiding dairy without deliberately substituting other sources, postmenopausal women (accelerated bone turnover), older adults generally, and people with restrictive eating patterns. Spreading calcium-rich foods across the day (rather than one large dose) may support absorption, since the body absorbs it most efficiently in moderate amounts at a time. Talk to your provider before supplementing, particularly regarding total daily amounts from food plus supplements combined.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Potassium — fluid balance, muscle function, and the sodium counterbalance
text: Potassium is the primary positively charged ion inside cells and works opposite sodium to regulate fluid balance, support healthy blood pressure, and enable normal muscle contraction and nerve transmission, including the heartbeat. Public health nutrition frames potassium and sodium as a functional pair: modern processed-food diets tend to run high in sodium and comparatively low in potassium, and shifting that ratio toward more potassium-rich whole foods is a well-supported, food-first lever for cardiovascular support. Rich whole-food sources include leafy greens, potatoes and sweet potatoes (especially with skin), white beans, bananas, avocado, tomatoes, oranges, and coconut water. Potassium is notably abundant and widespread across fruits, vegetables, and legumes, so a diet built around whole plant foods tends to naturally support intake — unlike some other minerals that concentrate in narrower food categories. People who commonly run low, educationally, include those eating primarily processed/packaged food (low in potassium, high in sodium), people on certain diuretic medications, those with gastrointestinal losses from vomiting or chronic diarrhea, and heavy exercisers with high sweat losses who don't replace electrolytes. A simple food-first pattern — a baked potato with skin, a banana, a big vegetable-forward meal — supports intake meaningfully. Potassium is one nutrient where supplement caution is especially warranted because excess can affect heart rhythm, particularly with reduced kidney function; talk to your provider before supplementing, and lean on whole foods as the primary strategy.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Vitamin C — antioxidant defense, collagen synthesis, and iron partnership
text: Vitamin C is a potent water-soluble antioxidant that supports collagen synthesis (relevant to skin, joints, and blood vessel integrity), immune cell function, and — notably — enhances the absorption of non-heme iron from plant foods when eaten in the same meal. Because humans cannot synthesize vitamin C, unlike most animals, consistent dietary intake matters. Rich whole-food sources go well beyond citrus: bell peppers (especially red), strawberries, kiwi, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, papaya, and dark leafy greens are all excellent sources, with red bell pepper and kiwi often exceeding orange juice per serving. Vitamin C is notably heat- and oxygen-sensitive — it degrades with prolonged cooking, cut-surface exposure to air, and long storage — so raw or lightly steamed preparation and eating produce reasonably fresh preserves more of it. Its antioxidant role also supports regenerating vitamin E back to its active form, illustrating how micronutrients function as an interdependent network rather than in isolation. People who commonly run low, educationally, include smokers (who have measurably higher vitamin C turnover and needs), people eating very few fruits and vegetables, those recovering from illness or wound healing, and people under high physiological stress. A practical food-first habit is pairing a vitamin C food with an iron-rich plant meal — bell pepper strips with lentil soup, a squeeze of lemon over spinach — to support absorption on both fronts. Talk to your provider before supplementing at high doses.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Iodine — the quiet mineral behind thyroid and metabolic regulation
text: Iodine is a core structural component of thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolic rate, energy production, and — during pregnancy and infancy — fetal and early brain development. It's a mineral that gets little everyday attention but is functionally essential in fairly small amounts. Whole-food sources include seaweed (kelp, nori, wakame — among the most concentrated sources by far), fish and other seafood, dairy (iodine enters milk partly via sanitizing agents used in dairy processing), and eggs; iodized salt has historically been the public-health backbone of iodine intake in many countries, so a shift toward non-iodized specialty salts (sea salt, Himalayan salt, kosher salt) without another iodine source can quietly reduce intake. Soil iodine content varies significantly by region, which historically drove goiter patterns before fortification programs. People who commonly watch their iodine status, educationally, include those who avoid iodized salt in favor of other salts without substituting seaweed or seafood, people following vegan diets without seaweed or fortified foods, pregnant and breastfeeding people (needs increase meaningfully), and those living in regions with naturally iodine-poor soil. Interestingly, iodine is a nutrient where more isn't automatically better — very high intake, particularly from concentrated seaweed, can also disrupt thyroid function, so food-first moderation (a few sheets of nori, occasional seafood, iodized salt in cooking) is the sensible frame rather than mega-dosing. Talk to your provider before supplementing, especially with any known thyroid condition.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Selenium — antioxidant enzyme cofactor and thyroid partner
text: Selenium is incorporated into selenoproteins, including glutathione peroxidase (a key antioxidant enzyme) and enzymes that activate thyroid hormone, giving it a supportive role in both antioxidant defense and thyroid function alongside iodine. It's one of the few nutrients where a single food can meet needs in one or two bites: Brazil nuts are extraordinarily concentrated in selenium, with even one to two nuts providing a substantial amount — a distinctive food-first talking point, though also a caution against overdoing them, since selenium has a narrower safe range than most minerals. Beyond Brazil nuts, good sources include seafood, organ meats, eggs, sunflower seeds, and, to a variable degree, whole grains and mushrooms, since plant selenium content depends heavily on the selenium level of the soil they're grown in (some regions, notably parts of China and central Africa, have naturally selenium-poor soil, while others, like much of the U.S. Midwest, are selenium-rich). This soil-dependence makes selenium somewhat different from most micronutrients discussed in food terms — geography matters more than food category. People who commonly watch selenium status, educationally, include those in regions with selenium-poor soil, people with very restrictive diets, and those with malabsorptive gut conditions. Because the gap between a supportive amount and an excessive one is narrower for selenium than for most minerals, a food-first approach — an occasional Brazil nut or two rather than daily handfuls, plus routine inclusion of seafood or eggs — is the sensible frame. Talk to your provider before supplementing.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Vitamin A & carotenoids — vision, skin integrity, and the plant-vs-animal distinction
text: Vitamin A supports healthy vision (particularly low-light adaptation), skin and mucosal barrier integrity, and immune function. Like folate, it exists in two meaningfully different dietary forms: preformed vitamin A (retinol), found in animal foods like liver, egg yolks, and dairy, is used directly by the body; provitamin A carotenoids — beta-carotene, alpha-carotene, and others — found in orange, yellow, and dark leafy plant foods (carrots, sweet potatoes, pumpkin, mangoes, spinach, kale) must be converted by the body into active vitamin A, and this conversion is somewhat variable between individuals and generally modest in efficiency. Carotenoids also function as antioxidants in their own right — independent of vitamin A conversion — and are linked with eye health, particularly lutein and zeaxanthin, which concentrate in the retina and are found in leafy greens, corn, and egg yolks. Because carotenoids are fat-soluble pigments, eating them with a source of fat (olive oil on roasted carrots, avocado with a spinach salad) meaningfully improves absorption compared to eating them fat-free. Cooking and lightly processing carotenoid-rich vegetables (blending, chopping, gentle cooking) also breaks down plant cell walls and improves bioavailability compared to raw. People who commonly watch vitamin A status, educationally, include those on very low-fat diets (impairing carotenoid absorption), people with fat-malabsorption conditions, and strict vegans relying solely on conversion-dependent carotenoids without any preformed sources. Talk to your provider before supplementing, since preformed vitamin A is fat-soluble and can accumulate to excess.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

title: Vitamin K — clotting, bone-calcium direction, and the K1/K2 distinction
text: Vitamin K supports normal blood clotting and plays a supportive role in bone metabolism by helping activate proteins (like osteocalcin) that direct calcium into bone rather than soft tissue and arteries — a functional-medicine talking point that connects vitamin K to cardiovascular and bone health together, not just clotting. There are two main dietary forms: vitamin K1 (phylloquinone), abundant in leafy greens (kale, spinach, collards, broccoli, Brussels sprouts) and the most common dietary form by far; and vitamin K2 (menaquinone), found in smaller amounts in fermented foods (natto is an exceptionally concentrated source), some cheeses, and egg yolks, and also produced in modest amounts by gut bacteria. K1 and K2 are metabolized somewhat differently in the body, and some integrative practitioners emphasize including both forms — leafy greens for K1, occasional fermented dairy or natto for K2 — rather than relying on K1 alone. Vitamin K is fat-soluble, so pairing leafy greens with a source of fat (olive oil dressing, avocado, nuts) supports absorption meaningfully, much like with carotenoids. People who commonly watch vitamin K status, educationally, include those eating very few leafy greens or cruciferous vegetables, people with fat-malabsorption conditions, and those on long-term antibiotic use (which can reduce gut bacterial K2 production). Vitamin K is one nutrient where consistency matters for a specific medical reason: anyone on blood-thinning medication should keep leafy-green intake steady rather than fluctuating, and should talk to their provider before making significant dietary changes or supplementing.
source: Linus Pauling Institute Micronutrient Information Center; NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
